etymology: From Latin desperare (to despair, to give up hope), through Old French desperat; appearing once in the Authorized Version, intensifying Jeremiah's indictment of the deceitfulness of the human heart.
biblical_def:
The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it?

Desperately appears once in the Authorized Version, in one of Jeremiah's most quoted single verses, intensifying wicked to the point of naming a condition beyond ordinary description or repair. The word does not describe an occasional lapse but a settled, thoroughgoing corruption — desperately here carries the older sense of beyond hope, incurable by any human remedy, not the modern sense of urgent effort. Jeremiah pairs this with deceitful above all things, so that the verse names two linked problems at once: the heart's corruption is not only severe but also hidden from the very person whose heart it is, which is why the question who can know it? follows immediately rather than any confident diagnosis. The verse stands near the head of Reformed anthropology's doctrine of total depravity, precisely because it refuses the comforting assumption that self-examination alone can uncover the heart's true state. The verse that follows in Jeremiah supplies the only adequate answer: I the LORD search the heart, I try the reins — what is desperately wicked and hidden from the man himself is not hidden from God, who alone can both diagnose and heal it.

corruption_summary: A therapeutic reading softens 'desperately wicked' into ordinary human imperfection or a call to greater self-awareness, missing that the verse's whole point is that the heart's corruption cannot be adequately diagnosed by the very self-examination such readings recommend.
corruption_paragraphs: A self-help gloss on this verse can turn it into encouragement toward deeper introspection — know your heart better and you will master its deceit — precisely inverting Jeremiah's point. The verse does not counsel more careful self-examination; it declares self-examination inadequate to the task, since the heart deceitful above all things deceives the examiner as readily as anyone else.

The historic Reformed reading of this verse is not a pessimistic invention but the text's own conclusion, confirmed in the next verse's turn to God as the only competent searcher of hearts. The principle to recover is that desperately wicked names a condition requiring external diagnosis and external remedy — the LORD's own searching and trying — rather than a project the sinner can complete by looking harder within himself.

etymology: From Old French gorgias (elegant, fine), possibly related to gorge (throat, ruff); appearing once in the Authorized Version, describing the robe Herod's soldiers mockingly placed on Jesus.
biblical_def:
Arrayed him in a gorgeous robe, and sent him again to Pilate.

Gorgeous appears once in the Authorized Version, in Luke's account of Jesus being sent by Pilate to Herod, who, with his men of war, set him at nought, mocked him, and arrayed him in a gorgeous robe before sending him back. The word names a robe of splendid, showy magnificence, and its use here is savagely ironic: the true King is dressed in royal finery not to honour Him but to make sport of Him, Herod's court treating the claim of kingship as a joke worth dressing up for laughter. Gorgeous carries no positive weight in this verse; it is mockery's chosen instrument, the very splendor of the garment measuring the depth of the contempt intended. Luke records, almost as an aside, that Herod and Pilate, previously at enmity between themselves, were made friends together that same day — a shared mockery becoming, however briefly, a point of political reconciliation. The gorgeous robe stands as one small but pointed detail in the passion narrative: the true King is arrayed in splendor, but only ever as an instrument of derision, until the true robe of honour is revealed at the resurrection.

The principle to recover is the verse's own irony: the gorgeous robe is not a tribute to Jesus but a weapon against Him, splendor weaponized as mockery. The passion narratives repeatedly use the trappings of kingship — a purple robe, a crown, a reed for a scepter — as instruments of derision, and this gorgeous robe belongs to that same pattern, true kingship recognized by its enemies only well enough to mock it.

etymology: Comparative degree of holy, from Old English halig; appearing once in the Authorized Version in the mouth of a rebellious people, spoken as a self-justifying boast rather than a true claim.
biblical_def:
Stand by thyself, come not near to me; for I am holier than thou.

Holier appears once in the Authorized Version, and its single occurrence is placed, with evident irony, in the mouth of the very people Isaiah is condemning. The prophet has just described a rebellious and gainsaying nation, one that sacrifices in gardens and burns incense upon altars of brick in open defiance of the law, and it is precisely this people whom Isaiah quotes as saying to others, stand by thyself, come not near to me; for I am holier than thou. The claim is not humility misapplied but self-righteousness weaponized — an outward show of ceremonial scrupulosity (refusing contact, maintaining ritual distance) used to justify contempt for others while the speaker's own idolatry goes unaddressed. Isaiah's next words expose the true weight of such a claim: these are a smoke in my nose, a fire that burneth all the day — not incense pleasing to God but an irritant provoking His judgment. Holier than thou stands permanently in Scripture as the classic biblical example of false, self-serving religious superiority, condemned in the very verse that records it being spoken.

The principle to recover is that Isaiah does not commend but condemns the claim: the speakers described are idolaters (sacrificing in gardens, eating swine's flesh) whose outward ritual distance from others masks rather than corrects their true condition before God. The verse teaches that a claimed holiness measured by distance from other people, rather than by conformity to God's law, is not holiness at all but a provocation — 'smoke in my nose' — however sincerely felt by the one who claims it.

etymology: From Latin commotio (a violent motion, agitation), from commovere (to move violently); appearing once as a plain noun in the Authorized Version, naming an invading army's disturbance out of the north.
biblical_def:
A great commotion out of the north country, to make the cities of Judah desolate.

Commotion appears once as a standalone noun in the Authorized Version, in Jeremiah's prophecy of the Babylonian invasion that will lay waste Judah's cities. The word names the noise, disturbance, and disorder of an advancing army — the noise of the bruit is come, and a great commotion out of the north country — announcing the approach of judgment through the plainest possible sensory description: something is heard before it is seen, a rising tumult that precedes the desolation it brings. The verse pairs commotion with a den of dragons, a figure for utter desolation and the haunt of wild creatures where cities once stood, so that the single word carries the whole movement from noise to ruin in one compressed image. Jeremiah's north country invaders are, throughout his prophecies, identified as the instrument of the LORD's own judgment on a covenant-breaking people; the commotion is not merely a political or military disturbance but the audible approach of a sentence long pronounced and now finally executed.

The verse teaches that what sounds, to an unwary ear, like mere noise and disorder may in fact be the LORD's own sentence arriving in plain, sensory form — heard before it is fully understood.

etymology: From Latin crudelis (hard, unfeeling), through Old French cruel; appearing once in the Authorized Version, naming the specific sin of a wicked father contrasted with his righteous son in Ezekiel's teaching on individual responsibility.
biblical_def:
As for his father, because he cruelly oppressed, spoiled his brother by violence... he shall die in his iniquity.

Cruelly appears once in the Authorized Version, in Ezekiel's teaching that each person bears responsibility for his own sin rather than inheriting guilt automatically from a parent. The chapter sets up a deliberate contrast: a righteous man has a violent son, and that same violent son in turn has a son who sees his father's sins and does not do likewise. Cruelly oppressed names precisely the wicked father's specific charge — active, violent extortion, spoiling his brother by violence — the concrete sin for which he alone will die in his iniquity, not passed down as inherited guilt to his own son who chooses differently. The word's single occurrence anchors one of the Old Testament's clearest statements against the proverb the chapter explicitly quotes and rejects — the fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children's teeth are set on edge — replacing inherited, unavoidable guilt with a doctrine of genuine individual moral responsibility before God, each soul answering for what it has itself done.

The principle to recover is the chapter's explicit argument: Ezekiel 18 quotes and rejects the proverb that children inevitably bear the guilt of their fathers' sins, insisting instead that the soul that sinneth, it shall die. etymology: From Old French dangereus, from dangier (power, dominion, hence peril); appearing once in the Authorized Version, describing the season of sailing during Paul's voyage to Rome.
biblical_def:
When sailing was now dangerous, because the fast was now already past, Paul admonished them.

Dangerous appears once in the Authorized Version, in Luke's careful nautical record of Paul's voyage toward Rome as a prisoner. The word marks a specific, calculable hazard — the fast (the Day of Atonement, marking the close of the safe sailing season in the ancient Mediterranean) had already past, making further sailing dangerous by the ordinary reckoning of experienced seamen. Paul, drawing on more than practical seamanship, admonished the ship's company against continuing the voyage, warning that this dangerous sailing would end not merely in loss of cargo but of lives, including his own. The centurion, however, believed the master and owner of the ship rather than Paul, and the voyage continued into the storm that Acts 27 narrates at length, ending in shipwreck exactly as Paul had warned — though, as Paul also promises during the storm, with the loss of no lives. Dangerous here names a real, physical peril accurately assessed and rightly warned against, one whose disregard brought exactly the consequences foretold, softened only by the mercy Paul had also promised alongside the warning.

The principle to recover is the narrative's own quiet lesson: Paul's assessment of dangerous sailing conditions was both spiritually and practically sound, yet the centurion trusted the ship's master and owner instead — worldly expertise over apostolic warning — and the ensuing shipwreck vindicated Paul's judgment exactly. The mercy that followed (every life preserved, as Paul also promised) shows that disregarded warning does not exhaust the patience of the God who gave it.

pos: v. (past tense, of DISAPPOINT, = frustrated, brought to nothing)
etymology: From Old French desappointer (to undo an appointment, to remove from office), through the notion of a plan or purpose overturned; appearing once in the Authorized Version, describing purposes that fail for want of counsel.
biblical_def:
Without counsel purposes are disappointed: but in the multitude of counsellors they are established.

Disappointed appears once in the Authorized Version, in one of Proverbs' many sayings on the necessity of wise counsel. The sense here is stronger than the modern, softer meaning of mild letdown; disappointed carries its older force of frustrated, brought to nothing, a plan actively undone rather than merely a hope gently unmet. The proverb states a plain contrast: purposes formed without counsel are disappointed, while those tested and refined through the multitude of counsellors are established, made to stand firmly rather than collapse. The verse belongs to a whole current of wisdom literature warning against the self-sufficiency of a single mind, however capable, set against the humility of seeking and weighing outside judgment before committing to a course of action. Disappointed here is not primarily about the emotional experience of the planner but about the objective fate of the plan itself — it fails to hold, comes apart under pressure, precisely because it was never tested against wiser counsel before being set in motion.

The principle to recover is the proverb's own plain contrast: purposes formed in isolation, however confidently held, are disappointed — brought to nothing — while purposes tested against a multitude of counsellors are established, made to stand. This is not a counsel of timidity but a warning against the particular self-sufficiency that refuses correction before it is too late to receive it.

etymology: From Old English forgietan (to lose the memory of), formed with the intensive for- prefix; appearing once in the Authorized Version, describing an honest oversight of gleaning law turned into a deliberate provision for the poor.
biblical_def:
When thou cuttest down thine harvest... and hast forgot a sheaf in the field, thou shalt not go again to fetch it.

Forgot appears once in the Authorized Version, in Deuteronomy's gleaning laws providing for the stranger, the fatherless, and the widow. The law envisions an entirely ordinary human failure — a harvester who has forgot a sheaf in the field, an honest oversight rather than a deliberate act of charity — and then legislates precisely that this ordinary mistake must not be corrected: thou shalt not go again to fetch it. What would in any other transaction be a loss to be recovered becomes, by divine command, a provision deliberately left in place for those who have no harvest of their own. The law converts an accident into an institution: the sheaf's owner is forbidden from reclaiming his own forgotten property specifically so that the poor may glean it, and the text supplies the motive directly — that the LORD thy God may bless thee in all the work of thine hands. Forgot here names the small, unplanned edges of ordinary labour that God's law claims for the needy, teaching that provision for the poor need not always be a special act of generosity but can be built into the ordinary carelessness of daily work, left uncorrected by design.

etymology: From Old French emprisoner, from prison; appearing once in the Authorized Version, in Paul's own recollection, before Christ, of his former persecution of the church.
biblical_def:
Lord, they know that I imprisoned and beat in every synagogue them that believed on thee.

Imprisoned appears once in the Authorized Version, in Paul's account of his vision in the temple at Jerusalem, recounted before Agrippa and elsewhere in his defense narratives. The word comes not from a narrator describing Paul's past but from Paul's own mouth, addressed directly to the risen Christ in prayer: Lord, they know that I imprisoned and beat in every synagogue them that believed on thee. The confession is remarkably specific and self-incriminating, offered as part of Paul's own argument to Christ that his testimony ought to be especially credible in Jerusalem precisely because his former zeal against believers was so well known. Christ's answer, recorded immediately after, is not to dispute the confession but to redirect Paul's mission entirely — depart: for I will send thee far hence unto the Gentiles. Imprisoned here stands as part of Paul's own unflinching record of his former violence against the church, offered not to excuse it but as evidence of how completely grace had since overturned it, the persecutor become the apostle to the very Gentiles he once had no thought of reaching.

The principle to recover is Paul's own model of honest confession: he does not soften or excuse his former persecution of the church when recounting it to Christ, but states it plainly — I imprisoned and beat — offering it as evidence of how thoroughly grace has since redirected him. The pattern teaches that conversion does not require forgetting or minimizing a genuinely bad past; it requires that past to be named honestly as the very ground on which grace's transforming work is measured.

etymology: From Latin infamis (of ill repute), from in- (not) + fama (fame, reputation); appearing once in the Authorized Version, describing Jerusalem's reputation among the surrounding nations because of her sin.
biblical_def:
Those that be near, and those that be far from thee, shall mock thee, which art infamous and much vexed.

Infamous appears once in the Authorized Version, in Ezekiel's oracle against Jerusalem, part of a chapter cataloguing the city's princes, priests, and people for shedding blood, oppressing the poor, and profaning holy things. The margin reading, Heb. polluted of name, much in vexation, clarifies the sense precisely: infamous here names not merely a bad reputation in the ordinary social sense but a name defiled, made unclean by the very conduct the chapter has just detailed. The judgment named is public and comprehensive — both those that be near and those that be far will mock a city whose infamy is no longer hidden but has become a byword among the nations she once might have instructed. Ezekiel's larger argument throughout this section of his prophecy is that Israel's calling was to be a light and a witness among the nations; infamous names the precise inversion of that calling, a people meant to display holiness instead displaying a defiled name that draws mockery rather than honour from every direction.

The principle to recover is the margin's own clarification: infamous here is polluted of name, a reputation earned through documented sin, not misfortune suffered unjustly. The chapter's long catalogue of specific offenses — bloodshed, oppression of the poor and the stranger, profaning the sabbath — makes plain that the mockery of near and distant nations answers a real defilement, the precise inversion of the calling to be a light among those very nations.
